Is a Medical background really less common among people who stay in social action?

A plain-language report for the NGO. Question 9 in the SEARCH / NIRMAN series. It brings together seven reports on this one theme and reads them as a whole.

The answer in two sentencesYes on the headline, but only if you say who Sustainers are being compared with: 28.8% of Sustainers studied Medical, against 50.0% of everyone else and 40.4% of people who started and then left. The headline gap is mostly a mix effect from Students and the Educational Break group, it reverses when Educational Break is left out, it fades once workshop batch is accounted for, and it is not the biggest difference between Sustainers and Early Leavers (workshop batch is).

1. The questions the NGO asked

Seven reports were produced, but they ask four different questions. Four of the seven (reports 1, 6, 0 and Step 5) ask the same one, run through two different workflows. The links open the live reports.

Question A: the core claim (reports 1, 6, 0 and Step 5)

"Medical stream (Pharmacy excluded) was less common among Sustainers. Use prodnirmandemographics. Useful fields: CurrentStatusOf_Work, EducationalStreamCategory, Participant_Id. Note: Educational_Stream should not be used for this claim. It holds values such as 'Medical / Public Health', which is a different definition and would change the counts."

Question B: Medical versus age, Sustainers against Early Leavers (report 3)

"Compared with Early Leavers, Sustainers are less often in the Medical EducationalStreamCategory and tend to have a higher AgeAtWorkshop. Validate this."

Question C: the 338-person cohort claim (report 2)

"In the 338-person cohort, about 85% of Early Leavers (120 of 142) are Medical stream. Medical is the biggest difference between Sustainers and Early Leavers in this data. Validate this."

Question D: the six-part check using years of social action (report 4)

Show the full question
"Using prodnirmandemographics, keep rows where PersonYearsOfSocialAction is not null, CurrentAge > 0, AgeAtWorkshop > 0, and CurrentAge minus AgeAtWorkshop >= 3. Check that N is about 338. Label Sustainer if PersonYearsOfSocialAction >= 3 (expect about 136) and Early Leaver if it is <= 1 (expect about 142). Drop the middle group (about 60). Then check: (1) the share of Sustainers within each EducationalStreamCategory, expecting Medical to be about 12% and the others about 79 to 90%; (2) the median AgeAtWorkshop per group, expecting about 24 vs 22; (3) WorkshopsAttendedCount per group; (4) Gender and NativeState after adjusting for AgeAtWorkshop; (5) CurrentStatusOfWork among Early Leavers, expecting about 65% Educational Break and 18% Social Impact Work; (6) repeat using only strict leavers (CurrentStatusOfWork not Educational Break or Social Impact Work, about 24 people). Do not claim cause and effect. Then re-run the questionnaire step (prodnirmanquestionnaire, WorkshopLevel 0.1, Pre vs Post) that returned no results."

2,890 participants in the demographics table. "Medical" means the stream category Medical, which leaves Pharmacy out. A Sustainer is someone whose current status is Social Impact Work; an Early Leaver is "Previously SIW".

2. The short answer

"Medical was less common among Sustainers" is true as a description, but it is not a clean finding. Always say what the comparison group is.

Every report that looked at the same people got the same counts, so the numbers are solid. What differs is the story told about them. The consistency reports call the claim supported because five methods agree on one comparison. The discovery reports ask whether it survives a change of comparison group, and find it does not fully: one small, Medical-heavy group (Educational Break) decides the direction. Against Early Leavers directly the link is modest and weakens after batch is controlled. The two follow-up claims did worse: the 338-person figures could not be reproduced, and the age claim is inconclusive.

Think of it like comparing one team's height with "everyone else". If "everyone else" includes a basketball squad, the gap says more about who is in the pool than about the team. Here the basketball squad is the Educational Break group, and the pool is also full of Students who have not yet had time to settle on a path.

4. Was it a meaningful discovery?

Reading all seven reports together, the findings fall into three groups. Where the reports differ, it is in how strongly they word the same numbers, not in the numbers themselves.

Meaningful

Medical is under-represented among Sustainers, and the counts are rock solid

Six of the seven reports reproduce the same group counts (136 of 473, 1,209 of 2,417, 40 of 99, N = 2,890). Sustainers are about 21 points less Medical than everyone else, and about 12 points less than Early Leavers (odds ratio 0.60, range 0.38 to 0.93). It is an association only, since there is no comparison group.

Confirmed, but weaker than it sounds

"Supported, 100% agreement" is not the same as "robust"

Reports 1 and 6 show five methods agreeing on one comparison, but their own text says most of the 21-point gap comes from Students and Educational Break, and among experienced statuses the gap is small and not significant (a stricter check gives odds ratio 0.81, range 0.63 to 1.04). The discovery reports go further: the result reverses when Educational Break (88.6% Medical) is dropped, the key test is borderline (adjusted p 0.0495, about 0.057 under Fisher's test, by the analyst's own calculation), and it fades once batch is controlled in the Early Leaver comparison (p 0.18). So "Exceptional confidence" in reports 1 and 6 overstates; the discovery wording, "Conditional, 80% confidence", fits the evidence better.

Not confirmed, inconclusive or never answered

The 338 / 85% claim, the age claim and the six-part check

The 338-person figures and the "85% of Early Leavers are Medical" claim do not match the data (40.4%, not 84.5%), and Medical is not the biggest difference: batch is. "Sustainers are older" is inconclusive (+0.75 years, fragile, and it reverses after batch adjustment). Report 4 produced no analysis at all, so its benchmarks (12% Medical, 24 strict leavers, Pre/Post changes) are unchecked. Inside the discovery report, Steps 2, 3 and 5 returned no key metrics (Step 2's narrative gave numbers, Steps 3 and 5 gave none), so the bootstrap, permutation and leave-one-batch-out checks were never run.

What is safe to say"Sustainers were somewhat less often Medical (28.8%) than other graduates with a settled non-Sustainer outcome (35.3%; batch-adjusted odds ratio about 0.76, range 0.59 to 0.97), and less often than Early Leavers (28.8% vs 40.4%, a gap that fades once batch is controlled). Much of this comes from the Educational Break group, which is 88.6% Medical. Without that group, Sustainers were somewhat more often Medical. This is an association, not a cause."

What not to say

  • "Sustainers are less likely to be Medical", with no comparison group named. The sign changes with the group.
  • "50% vs 28.8%" as if it were an effect. It mostly reflects the Student and Educational Break mix.
  • "Medical students are less likely to stay" or any wording that predicts or causes. Reversing the view is the same table, not a second proof.
  • "Medical is the biggest difference" or "85% of Early Leavers are Medical". Neither is in the data.
  • "Sustainers are older". The evidence is inconclusive.
  • Using the 0.63 odds ratio as the headline. It adjusts for workshops attended, which may be a result of being active.

In short: a true and reproducible description, a direction that depends on one small group, a modest and fragile link to Early Leaving, and several claims that are either wrong or unanswered. Discovery confidence is 80% for "conditional", not for the claim itself.

NIRMAN programme directors: what this means

NIRMAN is run by SEARCH with MKCL to find and support young people who want to work on social problems. In this data, "Sustainer" means someone whose current status is Social Impact Work, and "Early Leaver" means someone who engaged and then left.

What the data says to you

  • Do not use study stream to pick or screen people. The Medical link is modest, depends on the comparison and fades after cohort timing is accounted for. The report itself says not to use it for targeting or selection.
  • Timing matters more than stream. Workshop batch is the largest difference between Sustainers and Early Leavers. Recent batches have had less time to show an outcome, so they can look more "sustained" than they are.
  • Define "Educational Break". This group of 167 is 88.6% Medical, has no dates, and alone decides whether the claim holds. The schema treats it as "leaning positive", but nobody yet knows whether it means a pause, a drop-out or a step before returning.
  • Check the source of the 338 / 142 / 120 figures before quoting them anywhere. They do not match this table.

These describe patterns, not the effect of the workshop, because there is no comparison group. Programme background is from the NIRMAN website.

Four questions, seven reports. The order below is logical, not the order they were run. The core claim went through two workflows (a discovery and a five-method consistency check); the follow-up claims about Early Leavers each went through the consistency check; the last question never produced output.

Two cross-checks hold up. Report 2 says Medical raises the odds of being an Early Leaver by 1.68; report 3 says it lowers the odds of being a Sustainer by 0.60. These are the same 2x2 table read in opposite directions (1 / 1.68 is about 0.60), so they agree. Also, the five runs in each report use the same participants, so they show consistency, not independent proof.

8. The discovery's decision path (human in the loop)

At each step the AI proposed next moves and one was chosen. Only two of the five steps produced usable key metrics, which is why the verdict rests on Step 1 and Step 4.

Results returned1. Data check and base crosstabChoice: censor-aware primary contrast with interval estimates
Narrative only, not in key metrics2. Medical prevalence against each comparison groupChoice: batch-stratified adjustment with decomposition
No output3. Batch adjustment and older-batch restrictionChoice: merge into the Step 4 model
Results returned4. Adjusted models, with and without Educational BreakChoice: robustness verdict built around Educational Break
No output5. Six-specification robustness matrixChoice: re-run with hard-fail guards

Step 5 returned nothing, so the bootstrap, permutation, leave-one-batch-out and fragility checks do not exist. The only Step 5 numbers are crude counts: three specifications point lower (S1, S3, S5) and three point higher (S2, S4, S6). Those come from counts alone.

11. Things to keep in mind

  • No comparison group and an undated snapshot. Everyone attended, and Current_Status_Of_Work has no transition dates, so none of this shows the workshop caused anything. Recent batches are censored.
  • Agreement is not the same as robustness. The "100% agreement" in the consistency reports measures how many methods match on one comparison, not whether the comparison is the right one. Report 4 shows the extreme case: perfect agreement on an empty result.
  • Educational Break is undefined. It could be a pause, a drop-out or a step before returning. Putting it in or out of the comparison is a judgement call that decides the direction.
  • The discovery has gaps. Steps 2, 3 and 5 returned no key metrics. The unreported model without workshops attended (M2b), the older-batch restriction and the full robustness matrix are all still to be run.
  • Small groups. Early Leavers number 99 (62 with a known age), Not Sure 35. Intervals for the Early Leaver gap stop about 1 point from zero, and report 3 applied no correction for many tests.
  • Age is missing for about a third. Age_At_Workshop is 0 (unknown) for 31 to 37% of rows, so the age claim rests on a non-random subset.
  • Definitions matter. Medical here excludes Pharmacy and uses Educational_Stream_Category. Using Educational_Stream ("Medical / Public Health") would change the counts. Sustainer here is the status Social Impact Work, not "3 or more years of social action", which was only planned in report 4.
  • Open items, in priority order: define Educational Break; re-run report 4 with data loaded; run the model without workshops attended; run the missing robustness checks; find where 338 / 142 / 120 came from.
